tabDesc.capability: Current state of static rules and LightAgent

capability.intro: frago injects guidance into the agent on every prompt submission, in two layers: static rules are always in effect, while LightAgent only exists once a model profile is configured. Below is what each layer is actually doing right now.
capability.loadFailed: Failed to read prompting capability status.
capability.saveFailed: The switch was not saved; the configuration is unchanged.

static.name: Static rules
static.lede: Routing rules compiled into the frago-core binary, matched by event and injected directly, with no model involved.
static.count: {{total}} rules are matching, built-in and user rules combined; the decision takes tens of milliseconds.
static.countUnknown: The rule count could not be read right now; matching itself is unaffected.
static.noConfigNeeded: This layer needs no configuration and consumes no model quota.

ai.name: LightAgent
ai.lede: On every prompt submission, the last few turns of the conversation are sent to a cheap model along with the rule, book, and knowledge-domain indexes, which returns one line of guidance to inject.

body.enabled: Currently using {{model}}. Each prompt submission adds one call to that model.
body.disabled: This layer was turned off by hand — nothing is broken. Flip the switch below to bring it back.
body.not_configured: No usable model profile was found, so this layer has never been called.
body.no_key: The api key on profile {{profile}} is empty, so this layer cannot reach a model.

consequence.not_configured: Consequence: no guidance generated from your recent turns will appear in the session. Static rules are unaffected and keep working.
consequence.no_key: Consequence: this layer does nothing at all, and it is only one key short of working. The engine skips it outright when the key is empty — no request is sent. Static rules are unaffected.

ai.switchDesc: When off, frago no longer calls a model for guidance; static rules keep working.
ai.persistence: The switch is written to <c>hook_review.enabled</c> in <c>~/.frago/config.json</c>, the same field the engine reads; a missing section counts as on.
ai.envOff: The environment variable <c>FRAGO_REVIEW=off</c> is in effect and overrides this switch: LightAgent will not run in this environment, and the switch above has no effect for now.

githubGuard.bannerNotInstalledTitle: GitHub CLI is missing — nothing here is backed up
githubGuard.bannerNotInstalledText: frago uses the GitHub CLI to sync your working directory to a private repository of your own — free, private, visible only to you. Without it, your recipes, skills and session history exist on this machine and nowhere else.
githubGuard.bannerNotAuthTitle: GitHub CLI is installed but not logged in
githubGuard.bannerNotAuthText: Once you log in, frago can create your private repository and sync your working directory to it — and community recipe access goes from 60 requests an hour to 5000.
githubGuard.why1: A free private backup: frago creates a private repository under your own account and syncs your working directory into it. The repository is yours; the contents stay private.
githubGuard.why2: Nothing lost when you switch machines: log in with the same account on a new computer and your recipes, skills and settings come back as they were.
githubGuard.why3: No more rate-limited community recipes: anonymous GitHub access allows 60 requests an hour, shared across everyone on your IP. Logged in, it is 5000.
githubGuard.noAccountText: Signing up is free and takes about two minutes — an email address is all it needs. Private repositories are free too, with no limit on how many.
githubGuard.planTitle: How this machine will install it
githubGuard.planBrew: Using the Homebrew you already have: brew install gh. It lands on your normal PATH.
githubGuard.planWinget: Using Windows' built-in winget to install GitHub.cli. It lands on your normal PATH.
githubGuard.planBinary: No package manager is available here, so frago downloads GitHub's official release and unpacks it into ~/.frago/tools/gh/bin. No admin rights needed.
githubGuard.installRunning: Installing. This can take a few minutes — leave this page open.
githubGuard.pathHintTitle: Let your own terminal find gh too
githubGuard.pathHintText: frago calls its own copy directly and is unaffected. If you want to type gh at a prompt, add it to your PATH:
githubGuard.manualText: Run this in a terminal — same result:
githubGuard.manualDownload: Or download an installer from the official site:
githubGuard.step1Title: 1. frago asks GitHub for a one-time pairing code
githubGuard.step1Text: Press the button below and frago runs gh auth login on this machine. GitHub hands back an eight-character code, good for this one login and only for a few minutes.
githubGuard.step2Title: 2. You type that code into github.com
githubGuard.step2Text: The code and a link appear right here. Open the link, sign in to your GitHub account, and enter the code. Any device will do — your phone works.
githubGuard.step3Title: 3. GitHub asks you to authorize the GitHub CLI
githubGuard.step3Text: It lists the permissions being granted (repository access, workflows, and so on). Check that the app being authorized is GitHub CLI — that is GitHub's own tool.
githubGuard.step4Title: 4. The credential stays on your computer
githubGuard.step4Text: Once authorized, gh writes the token into this machine's keychain or credential manager. The token never leaves this machine, and frago never sends it anywhere.
githubGuard.starting: Asking GitHub for a pairing code…
githubGuard.codeLabel: Enter this pairing code on GitHub
githubGuard.waiting: Waiting for you to authorize on GitHub — this turns green by itself once you do.

team.startFreshWhy: Start something new together from nothing.
team.freshOpeningWhy: A session only exists once it has a first line — the platform takes no empty ones. Edit this as you like.
team.freshOpeningDefault: I've just paired up with a teammate. We'll work on this together. Stand by.
team.freshNeedOpening: The opening line can't be empty
team.waitStepId: Waiting for it to report its id
team.waitStepCode: Asking the relay for a code
team.waitIdFast: This one's id is there the moment it starts.
team.waitIdSlow: This one assigns its own id — usually 3–15 seconds, up to 30.
team.waitWhyNoCode: No code until the id is in hand: hand out a code first and your teammate walks into a session that isn't there yet.
team.waitCancelled: Stopped. The session that just started is still there — find it on the sessions page.
team.codeGiveIt: Send it to your teammate — they type it in and they're here
team.peerAwayWhy: They show up here once they type in the code above. This side carries on regardless.
team.instructTitle: Ask their agent to do something
team.instructWhy: This lands in their session as a user turn, carrying a line that says it came from you.
team.instructPlaceholder: What should their agent do… (⌘/Ctrl + Enter to send)

agent.notInstalled: Not found on this machine — install it and it shows up here by itself
agent.notReadable: frago can drive it, but its session records don't reach the workbench, so it would never appear in the left rail
agent.unknownInstall: This one offers no way to probe for it, so whether it's installed can't be told
agent.noKernel: frago's kernel isn't installed yet (nothing under ~/.frago/bin) — run frago init once
agent.noConnection: CoreAgent has no connection yet — pick one for it under connections in settings, or it can't reach a model
